headline: Refuse the universal tags X.680 assigns to no type, and tell a caller which those are.
summary: A DER element carrying a universal tag that no ASN.1 type is assigned to is not an encoding of anything, and the decoder was handing two ranges of them back as ordinary elements while the encoder was willing to write them. X.680 Table 1 reserves three rows: tag 0 for the encoding rules, tag 15 for future editions of the Recommendation, and tag 37 upward for its addenda. Tag 0 was already refused on the way in for the end-of-contents encoding it carries; tag 15 and everything from 37 up now are too, with `asn1/reserved-tag`, and all three are refused on the way out as well, so neither direction produces bytes the other calls malformed. The rule is read off the assignment table rather than off the set of types this codec has readers for, which is the smaller set: ObjectDescriptor, REAL, RELATIVE-OID, the time type, VideotexString, GraphicString and GeneralString are all assigned, all opaque here, and all still accepted inside an `ANY`.

Added: `pki.asn1.reservedUniversalTag(tagNumber)` answers whether X.680 reserves a universal tag number, which is the question `pki.asn1.decode` asks before it accepts an element. It returns `false` for every assigned type, including the seven this codec carries no reader for, so it is not a statement about what can be read: a caller deciding whether bytes are worth passing on gets the same answer the decoder will give. A value that is not a tag number answers `false` rather than throwing, as `pki.asn1.isPrintableString` and `pki.oid.isDottedDecimal` do of a value of the wrong type, and the type is checked before anything is compared, so `37.5` and `Infinity` are not read as reserved for sitting inside the addenda range and no `valueOf` of a caller's object is invoked inside the predicate.
Changed: `pki.asn1.decode` refuses a universal tag 15 element and any universal tag from 37 up, with `asn1/reserved-tag` naming the row of X.680 Table 1 that reserves it. Every reader in the toolkit inherits the refusal, so a message carrying such an element is refused at its own verb: `pki.schema.parse` and `pki.schema.detectFormat` report `schema/bad-der` before any format detector reads the children, which matters because a child nothing refuses is a child a detector may count. `pki.inspect.asn1` still prints the header walk beside the refusal, so an operator can see what the bytes claimed. Nothing that was accepted before and is assigned by X.680 changed: the four long-form time types and the two internationalized-resource-identifier types at tags 31 to 36 decode as they did.

`pki.asn1.encode` and `pki.asn1.encodeIdentifier` refuse the same tags, with the same `asn1/reserved-tag` code, rather than emitting bytes this toolkit's own decoder calls malformed. The class is read off the masked identifier bits as the decoder reads it, so a `classBits` carrying only the constructed bit is the universal class here too. Every other class is untouched, which is what makes the rule narrow enough to be safe: a context `[15]` is how an optional field is written across X.509 and CMS, and it encodes as it did. So do the assigned universal types at tags 31 to 36. The DER form restrictions are deliberately not enforced at this door: a constructed OCTET STRING or character string is a legitimate BER encoding that DER alone narrows to the primitive form, and this low-level encoder is how those bytes are minted for the BER reader that accepts them. A tag number that encodes nothing is a different matter from a form one set of encoding rules permits and another does not.

`pki.asn1.encode` and `pki.asn1.encodeIdentifier` require `classBits` to be a number naming a class: `0x00` universal, `0x40` application, `0x80` context or `0xc0` private, with `0x20` constructed allowed alongside. Anything else is `asn1/bad-tag`, as a tag number of the wrong type already was. The low five bits of that argument were being written into a single-octet identifier, so a value carrying any of them emitted a tag other than the one passed: `encodeIdentifier(0x0e, false, 1)` wrote `0f`, universal 15. A value that was not a number was narrowed into a class instead of refused, so `"128"` and `0x100000080` both encoded as a context `[1]`. For every argument still accepted the bytes are unchanged. A tag number past the four-octet high-tag form now reports `asn1/tag-too-large` ahead of any reserved-tag refusal, which is the order `pki.asn1.decode` has always refused that input in.

`pki.asn1.TAGS` is frozen. Assigning to it reached the encoders that compose an identifier from a tag number and the comparisons that test one against it, so a single assignment moved what a SEQUENCE is for every caller in the process. The numbers are X.680's; read them, and build a structure with a tag of your own through `pki.asn1.encode`.

Eight places that reported a failure by reading `message` off whatever was thrown now describe the thrown value the way the rest of the toolkit does. `pki.cmc.build`, `pki.cmp` session and verification, and `pki.crmf` are the verbs affected, and only the text of a message changes, in the case where what was caught is not an error or carries no readable message: it is named by its type instead of by a fixed phrase, and a `message` that answers from an accessor is read once rather than twice, so the text reported is the text that was tested. A `message` accessor that throws no longer replaces the failure being reported with its own. The error codes are unchanged.

A caught value whose `message` is the empty string is described by its type as well. It was being reported as the empty string it was, which left the sentence built around it ending at its colon with nothing after it. This reaches every message assembled that way, including the ones `pki.ocsp.httpRequest` and the revocation fetcher build. A message of only whitespace is still a message and is reported unchanged.
